title: Introduction; family background; parents' history
description: Cathy Naugle introduces Millie (Martha) Burroughs. Millie describes her birth in Lebanon, Ohio in 1899, her maiden name (Cromly, Anglicized from Bramlach), her mother's English-Scotch-Irish ancestry, her father's German ancestry, and her father's birth in eastern Tennessee during the Civil War.

title: Mother's family; women's restricted opportunities; grandparents
description: Millie describes her mother being denied the right to work by her father, her grandmother's domineering nature, her parents' unhappy marriage due to opposing interests, and her father's family history and the Civil War foraging raids.

title: Father's education; forestry career; family traits
description: Millie reads from her book about her grandfather John, his education at Johns Hopkins, his interest in trees, and his transition to a state forester. She also mentions her brother's business success and her father's remarriage after her mother's early death.

title: Millie's schooling; social isolation; prep department
description: Millie explains her unconventional education—being placed in first grade at age six-and-a-half, social isolation, double promotions, and attending a prep department with older women needing education to meet new teaching requirements.

title: First female rural mail carrier; World War I examination
description: Millie recalls how she became the first female rural mail carrier in the country during World War I after taking an examination, working a 27-mile route for a year and a half despite her mother's preference for this over auto mechanics.

title: Mail route experiences; horses; public reception
description: Millie details her daily mail route with eight-hour runs in good weather, challenges with mud and hills, using draft horses sharp-shod for ice, receiving food from patrons at Christmas, and the positive letter from postmaster E.R. Lash.

title: Graduate education; psychology training
description: Millie recounts earning her master's degree at Clark University in one year, followed by a year of Stanford-Binet testing experience at the Massachusetts School for the Feebleminded under Dr. Fernald's training system.

title: Mother's death; move to Columbus; juvenile research work
description: Millie Burroughs explains that her mother died of breast cancer after refusing examination, which led her to leave Clark and take a job at the Bureau of Juvenile Research in Columbus, Ohio. She describes doing mental testing and social work with delinquent and dependent children there.

title: Identity crisis; correspondence; marriage and mountain honeymoon
description: After her mother's death Burroughs realizes she has been living her mother's life vicariously and has an identity crisis. She resigns, heads west, meets Robert Ira Burroughs after corresponding by mail, and they marry in January 1929, spending the winter snowshoeing and hiking in a mountain cabin.

title: Husband's background; Appalachian migration; division of labor
description: She discusses her husband's Virginia origins, his journey west on freight trains, and his various jobs before wheat farming. She also comments on Appalachian migration patterns and explains how they divided labor based on physical strength, with him doing washing while she ran the tractor.

title: Parents' marriage; sex education; husband's first marriage
description: Burroughs talks about her parents' uncongenial marriage and her mother's negative view of marriage, her own late maturation and sex education from psychology books, and her husband's brief first marriage before World War One.

title: Daughters' high school; move to Saint Mary's; sawmill work
description: The family moves near Saint Mary's so her daughters Florence and Ruth can attend high school there; Burroughs takes an apartment and works washing dishes to support them while visiting her husband on weekends.

title: Daughters graduate; teaching at industrial school; husband's illness
description: After the daughters graduate in 1948, Florence goes to McGill and Ruth to Reed. To earn money Burroughs teaches at a reform school where conditions are impossible, then at Tensed and Rathdrum while her husband suffers a heart attack, spends a year in hospital and nursing home, and dies.

title: Widowhood; daughters' marriages; finances and depression years
description: She adjusts to widowhood by returning to teaching immediately, and discusses Ruth's marriage, leaving and returning to college, having eight children, and Florence's war marriage, divorce, and career as a veterinarian, along with the family's financial struggles during the depression.

title: Sex education for daughters; temperance; women's suffrage
description: Burroughs describes answering her daughters' questions about sex as they asked, mentions her mother's temperance crusading, and recalls voting in her first election at 21 without being involved in the suffrage movement.

title: Rural vs urban life; nature of things; raising children
description: She states her preference for rural timber country, discusses the importance of library access in the country, and argues that rural life teaches children the nature of things through direct experience, unlike urban intellectual environments.

title: Climbing anecdote; farm women's equality; frustration at home
description: She tells of climbing a mountain with a New Yorker who ignored the trail, discusses how farm women are needed and equal in work, and describes her frustration at being stuck at home with children and keeping housework to a minimum.

title: Motherhood and housework; left-handedness
description: The interviewee feels housework interfered with motherhood and believes an eight-hour job would have made her a better mother. She discusses being naturally left-handed and her parents changing her handedness at age one, which she believes caused her physical awkwardness.

title: Stepmother's puritanism; writing books
description: She describes her stepmother's puritanical upbringing, sexual repression, and difficult wedding night. The conversation turns to her writing, including a murder mystery co-written with her husband and an unpublished account of an industrial school semester.

title: Bobbed hair controversy; teaching career
description: She recalls facing criticism for bobbed hair while working in Massachusetts in the 1920s. She describes starting teaching at age 48, moving between elementary, high school, and college levels, and teaching psychology at Cheney and Fairchild Air Force Base.

title: Family life differences; birth control
description: She compares her rural upbringing with her daughter Ruth's family in Oregon. The discussion covers contraception in the 1930s, including cocoa butter suppositories, rubbers, diaphragms, and illegal abortions.

title: Women's movement; retirement and independence
description: She expresses support for the women's movement while noting it can be overdone. She discusses her independent retirement, her daughter Florence's house, and her strong preference for living in her own home over nursing homes or retirement complexes.

title: Depression; wars; current era
description: The Depression affected her family's move to Ohio, but World Wars I and II had little personal impact. She views the current era as a replay of the 1920s, with similar delinquency, drug issues, and intellectual movements.

title: Atomic war concerns; Stanford and book publication
description: She worries about atomic war and nuclear material hijacking. She reflects on nearly getting a job at Stanford with Terman's gifted child study, meeting her husband instead, and discusses the imminent publication of her book Restraints on Excellence.
